documents.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive Question Answering
documents.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on NLP Systems (ICNLP)
documents.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines a neural retriever with a sequence-to-sequence generator so that language model outputs are grounded in retrieved documents rather than only in the model's frozen parameters. The retriever is a Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) module that selects the top-k passages from a large text collection for a given query, and the generator is a BART-based model that conditions its output on both the original question and those passages. In our experiments, RAG outperformed a parametric-only baseline on open-domain question answering benchmarks such as Natural Questions and TriviaQA. We observed that grounding generation in retrieved evidence reduces hallucination: the model states facts that appear in the source passages instead of inventing plausible but unsupported details. Retrieval also allows the system to be updated by changing the document index, without retraining the generator. The main failure mode we identified is retrieval failure: if the retriever returns irrelevant passages, the generator may ignore the context and fall back to parametric knowledge, which reintroduces factual errors. RAG was published in 2020 and has since become the standard architecture for grounded question answering systems.

documents.title: SummaC: Sentence-Level Factual Consistency Detection using Natural Language Inference
documents.text: Factual inconsistency in generated summaries is often local: a single sentence may contradict the source document while the rest of the summary is correct. SummaC therefore performs verification at the sentence level rather than at the document level. For each sentence in the generated summary, we compare it against each sentence of the source document using a pretrained Natural Language Inference (NLI) model. NLI models classify a premise-hypothesis pair into one of three labels: entailment, contradiction, or neutral. Entailment means the evidence supports the sentence, contradiction means the evidence disagrees with it, and neutral means the evidence neither supports nor refutes it. We aggregate these pairwise scores into a single document-level consistency score and show that it correlates strongly with human judgments of factual consistency. Our approach requires no task-specific fine-tuning when a sufficiently strong pretrained NLI model is used. On the SummaEval and FactCC evaluation sets, sentence-level NLI scoring outperformed embedding-similarity baselines such as BLEU and ROUGE, which measure only surface overlap and fail to detect logically contradictory statements.

documents.title: RAGTruth: A Span-Level Corpus for Hallucination Detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
documents.text: Hallucination detection in RAG systems requires data at a finer granularity than whole-response labels. RAGTruth is a corpus in which annotators marked the exact word-level spans of hallucinated content inside more than eighteen thousand responses generated by retrieval-augmented language models. Each response is paired with the retrieval context that was supplied to the model, so a detector can learn to distinguish content that is supported by the context from content that is merely fluent. The annotation scheme distinguishes fully supported statements, unsupported additions, and statements that directly contradict the retrieval context. Analysis of the corpus shows that most hallucinations in RAG outputs are partial: models typically restate the retrieved context correctly and then append an extra detail, a citation to a non-existent source, or an inflated statistic. The corpus was released in 2024 and is now widely used for training and evaluating sentence-level and span-level hallucination detectors. Fine-tuning a DeBERTa-based NLI model on the RAGTruth training split produced large gains over the zero-shot baseline in our experiments.

documents.title: SelfCheckGPT: Reference-Free Detection of Hallucinations via Sampling Consistency
documents.text: SelfCheckGPT is a reference-free method for detecting hallucinations that does not require access to a knowledge base. The idea is to sample several independent responses from the same language model for the same question and then measure how consistent the target response is with those samples. If a statement in the target response is factually correct, it tends to reappear across most samples; if it is hallucinated, it is contradicted or omitted in the other samples. Consistency can be measured with sentence embeddings, n-gram overlap, or BERTScore. Because the method needs no external documents, it is easy to deploy, but it can only detect inconsistencies with the model's own distribution of beliefs, so systematic errors shared by all samples go undetected. This is an important limitation compared with evidence-based verification, which checks answers against retrieved documents. SelfCheckGPT achieves strong correlation with human hallucination annotations on the BioDomain and NarrativeQA evaluation sets.

documents.title: HaluEval: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Evaluating Hallucinations in Large Language Models
documents.text: HaluEval is a benchmark dataset for measuring how often and in what ways large language models hallucinate. The benchmark contains tens of thousands of samples covering question answering, dialogue summarization, and knowledge-grounded generation, each labelled as hallucinated or non-hallucinated. Half of the samples were produced by prompting a large language model to deliberately hallucinate, and the other half were collected from human-written responses. We evaluated several detection strategies on HaluEval, including direct prompting of a judge model, embedding similarity against the source document, and fine-tuned NLI classifiers. Our results show that judge models are inexpensive but over-confident, while fine-tuned classifiers give the best precision. HaluEval also provides a user study showing that readers are frequently unable to identify hallucinations without side-by-side access to the source context. The benchmark is intended as a general-purpose evaluation resource rather than a domain-specific one.

documents.title: FActScore: Fine-Grained Atomic Fact Evaluation of Generated Biographies
documents.venue: International Journal of Unverified AI Research (IJUAR)
documents.text: FActScore evaluates generation quality by decomposing a long-form response into a list of atomic facts, each expressing exactly one verifiable claim. Every atomic fact is then checked independently against a knowledge source such as Wikipedia, and the fraction of supported facts is reported as the factual precision of the response. This decomposition makes it possible to localise errors to specific sentences instead of scoring the whole document at once. In experiments on biographies of public figures, FActScore found that the average factual precision of the largest open models was below eighty percent, with errors concentrated in dates, quantities, and lesser-known affiliations. Atomic-level scoring was also more stable under prompt variation than document-level scoring. The method requires a reliable retrieval step: when the knowledge source lacks the relevant entry, correct statements are wrongly marked as unsupported, which inflates the measured error rate. Despite this limitation, atomic fact scoring is now a standard evaluation protocol for long-form generation.

documents.title: HHEM: The Hughes Hallucination Evaluation Model for Production RAG Systems
documents.text: The Hughes Hallucination Evaluation Model (HHEM) is a production-oriented classifier that estimates the probability that a summarization or RAG response is faithful to its source document. HHEM is trained on a large corpus of document-summary pairs labelled for factual consistency and is distributed as an open model that can be run on commodity hardware. In Vectara's evaluation harness, HHEM reports hallucination rates in the range of one to five percent for well-configured summarization pipelines, with higher rates observed when the input document is long or the summary is aggressive. The model scores each response independently of the question, so it measures consistency with the document rather than answer relevance. HHEM is widely used as an industry baseline for comparing new hallucination detectors, and its main limitation is that it produces only a document-level score and does not localise the specific sentence responsible for the hallucination.

documents.title: Deep Learning for Automated Diagnosis in Medical Imaging: A Clinical Review
documents.text: Convolutional neural networks have been applied to the interpretation of chest radiographs, retinal fundus images, and histopathology slides with performance approaching that of specialist clinicians in controlled studies. In a multi-centre evaluation of a deep learning system for chest X-ray screening, the reported sensitivity was 94 percent with a specificity of 89 percent on a held-out test set of twelve thousand images. Clinicians using the model as a decision support tool completed case reviews faster than clinicians working without assistance, although the study also documented a risk of automation bias, where readers accepted incorrect model suggestions. Regulatory approval for such systems requires external validation on data from hospitals outside the development site, because performance degrades when imaging protocols differ. The review concludes that imaging models should be deployed only with continuous monitoring for distribution shift, and that any clinical decision support answer must cite the study that supports it. All experiments described in this review received institutional ethics approval.
